newsitem.title: USA: Household product cos to see modest growth in '97.
newsitem.headline: Household product cos to see modest growth in '97.

text.p: Household product companies, which have felt pressure from a strong dollar and anemic top-line growth, are likely to sustain modest growth in 1997, analysts said.

During the past year, the dollar's strength in major markets like Japan and Germany as well as modest or even negative sales growth dragged down several key stocks, particularly the sector's powerhouse, Procter & Gamble Co.
Carol Warner, an analyst at Salomon Brothers, said P&G spent its fiscal year 1996 cutting costs and streamlining its internal structure while it absorbed low sales growth numbers.

"P&G's (1997) first quarter was by no means stellar and, in fact, the top line was downright disappointing," Warner said in a report. Salomon lowered its 1997 earnings estimate to $4.75 per share from $4.85 per share.

For the company's second quarter, Warner said she expected "modest" three percent sales growth. She said the company's switch to an everyday low pricing, or EDLP, strategy in Japan, its third largest market, is expected to hurt the company's numbers for several more quarters while retailers work through existing inventory.
Analysts said recent star performers like Clorox Co and Gillette Co are expected to lead the pack in 1997 with top-line growth.
Also, they said acquisitions made in the last year should help spur momentum in the new year.
"There have been a lot of acquisitions made and I think it is time to see some of these acquisitions paying off," said Michael Grant, a JP Morgan analyst.

For Clorox, analysts said the greatest challenge in 1997 is matching its recent performance of posting 10 percent volume growth each of the last three fiscal years. In the last quarter, the company had 15 percent volume growth and 14 percent sales growth.
In contrast, P&G's sales growth for the last quarter was negative one percent and Colgate-Palmolive Co's was six percent.
Warner said Clorox benefited from strong sales growth and not being exposed to some rivals' currency woes.
Gillette Co is another strong player this year, with new products like the clear stick anti-perspirant poised for strong sales.
"Clorox is up over 40 percent and so is Gillette and that is pretty good considering the market is up about 20 percent," Warner said.
Analysts said they expect Gillette to perform well in 1997 while it absorbs the acquisition of battery maker Duracell International Inc.
"I think in '97 they are going to take the Duracell products around the world as fast as possible. In the next few years we will see new products," said William Steele, a Dean Witter analyst.
Of all the consumer product stocks, analysts said Rubbermaid Inc has the greatest uphill battle in 1997.
The company was hard hit this past year by high resin costs and lagging sales in its Little Tikes kids' products.
Grant said he is looking for about nine percent sales growth for Rubbermaid's next quarter based mostly on its acquisition of Graco Children's Products Inc.
"I think in the near term their growth is going to be a little slow," Grant said. "Sales growth is not just going the way it needs to go."
Analysts said cosmetic stocks are on a great run, with new products from Revlon and Estee Lauder Cos Inc pushing sales upward and expansion into emerging markets broadening their customer base.

Regardless of what happens to the stock market in 1997, analysts said the sector will remain a desirable choice for investors because the companies offer strong and consistent earnings growth relatively unaffected by the economy's pace.
"I think overall in a market correction you are a little bit safer in the defensive names," said Grant.
((-- New York newsdesk 212-859-1610))
